That is what I have tried to give them across these ten chapters. It is a smaller gift than a name or a face would be. It is, I think, still worth giving.

section.subtitle: Judging the Judges
section.paragraph: A different kind of difficulty attends the other side of this history — the judges, interrogators, accusers, and officials whose decisions this book has traced in such institutional detail. I have tried throughout to avoid two opposite and, I think, equally inadequate responses to these figures. The first is to treat them as simply evil, a gallery of villains whose cruelty explains the whole catastrophe and whose motives require no further examination. This response is emotionally satisfying and historically false. The surviving record, as this book has shown repeatedly, is full of officials who appear, by every available indication, to have sincerely believed they were prosecuting a genuine and serious crime, operating within legal and theological frameworks that had absorbed centuries of careful, if ultimately mistaken, intellectual argument. Friedrich Spee's crisis of conscience, discussed in Chapter Five, was possible precisely because he was not a monster observing monsters; he was a sincere believer, doing his sincere duty as a confessor, who found himself unable to reconcile what he witnessed with what he already believed about justice and mercy. Treating every official in this history as a simple villain erases exactly the kind of complexity that makes Spee's story, and the stories of Weyer, Salazar, Scot, and Thomasius, actually instructive.

But the opposite response — the shrug of "they were simply products of their time," offered as though that fact settles the moral question rather than merely describing its circumstances — strikes me as equally inadequate, and in some ways more troubling, because it comes disguised as historical sophistication. People within this same period, operating with access to the same theological and legal traditions, reached different conclusions. Weyer read the confessions of the accused and saw illness. Spee heard the condemned in Bamberg and could no longer administer his own institution's sacraments without documenting his horror at what he had witnessed. Salazar examined the Basque testimony with a magistrate's trained skepticism and concluded that his own colleagues had been chasing phantoms. These were not people born into some different, more enlightened century, granted foreknowledge the rest of their era lacked. They were exact contemporaries of the officials who convicted, tortured, and executed, working from largely the same intellectual materials, who nonetheless arrived somewhere else. Their existence is, I think, the most important fact this book has to offer on the question of moral responsibility. It demonstrates that a different path was available, within the actual historical conditions of the period, to people who chose to take it. That does not make every official who failed to take it a monster. It does mean their failure was, in a meaningful sense, a choice, made within a world that contained visible alternatives, and I do not think the honest historian is required to withhold that judgment simply because it is uncomfortable to make about people who believed themselves righteous.

section.subtitle: The Courage of Doubt
section.paragraph: I have found myself, across the writing of this book, unexpectedly moved by the specific historical figures who make up what might be called this history's minor key — Weyer, Spee, Salazar, Scot, Bekker, Thomasius, the Parlement of Paris judges whose names mostly do not survive as individuals but whose collective pattern of appellate caution this book has traced across two chapters. None of them are conventional heroes. Weyer never fully abandoned belief in demonic power; he simply doubted its application to the specific women he saw accused. Spee's great intervention was, by his own account, born less of theological conviction than of the accumulated, unbearable weight of hearing condemned prisoner after condemned prisoner describe, in his role as their confessor, exactly how their confessions had actually been produced. Salazar did not set out to be a skeptic; he arrived at his conclusions through the unglamorous, methodical work of comparing testimony against testimony and finding the discrepancies his colleagues had been too eager to overlook.

I think there is something worth dwelling on in the unglamorousness of all of this. The popular imagination, when it reaches for stories of moral courage, tends to prefer the dramatic gesture — the public refusal, the defiant speech, the willingness to die for a principle loudly declared. What this book's record of dissent actually offers is something quieter and, I have come to think, more useful as a model: careful attention paid to evidence that made an official's own comfortable conclusions harder to sustain, and the willingness, once that attention had done its work, to say so in writing, to a professional and religious establishment not eager to hear it. Spee published his critique anonymously, not because his convictions were weak but because he understood exactly how dangerous stating them openly would be. Weyer wrote as a physician making a medical argument, not as a moral crusader. Their courage was not the courage of the barricade. It was the much less cinematic courage of continuing to look carefully at evidence that was increasingly difficult to look at, and of trusting that careful looking mattered even when the institutions around them were not yet ready to act on what it revealed.

section.subtitle: The Uncomfortable Mirror
section.paragraph: I want to be careful here, because this book has taken pains throughout to resist the temptation to flatten a specific, historically contingent institutional catastrophe into a generic parable about human nature that could apply, with equal force and equally little precision, to almost anything. The witch hunts were not simply an eternal human tendency wearing seventeenth-century dress. They were the product of a very specific fusion of theology, law, political fragmentation, and social circumstance, and Chapter Six's regional comparison exists precisely to demonstrate how much that specificity mattered — how the presence or absence of a functioning appellate court, a specific legal tradition, a specific configuration of political authority, determined whether a given community's ordinary human friction escalated into catastrophe or stayed, as it did in most places most of the time, at the level of unresolved local grudge.

And yet. I do not think it is a betrayal of that specificity to notice that certain of the mechanisms this book has traced in such careful institutional detail are not, in fact, confined to the particular centuries and courts this book has examined. The tendency of an interrogation, once convinced of its own conclusion, to shape the testimony it collects rather than genuinely test it. The tendency of institutions under internal or external pressure to treat the resolution of a case, rather than its accuracy, as the measure of success. The tendency of accusation, once it acquires enough social momentum, to become extremely difficult to interrupt regardless of the quality of the evidence sustaining it. The tendency of fear, in a community or a nation under genuine and unresolved strain, to seek a locatable cause rather than sit with genuine uncertainty. None of these tendencies, described at this level of generality, belongs uniquely to early modern Europe. This book has been careful, throughout, not to claim that any specific modern institution or event simply is a witch hunt in the full, historically loaded sense this book has spent ten chapters defining with precision. But I do not think the careful historian is required to pretend these underlying human and institutional tendencies vanished along with the specific demonological framework that once organized them. They did not disappear. They were, for a period of European history this book has documented in detail, organized with unusual completeness and unusual consequence. The organizing framework changed. I am considerably less confident that the underlying tendencies did.

section.subtitle: What History Cannot Give Us
section.paragraph: I want to close this reflection with a genuine limitation, rather than a tidy resolution, because I think tidiness would be its own kind of dishonesty after everything this book has tried to say about the danger of stories that resolve too neatly. For all the careful archival work this book has drawn upon, for all the demographic pattern, legal procedure, and regional comparison assembled across its ten chapters, there remains an irreducible distance between the historian's reconstruction and the actual, specific, unrecoverable experience of any single person who lived through what this book describes. We can establish, with real confidence, how the machinery worked. We can establish, with somewhat less confidence but still real evidentiary grounding, why it worked more severely in some places than others. We cannot establish, for the overwhelming majority of the people this book has been about, what it actually felt like to be inside it — the specific texture of a specific person's fear, hope, resignation, or faith, in a specific cell, on a specific night, centuries before anyone thought to ask them and record the answer in a form that might survive.

I do not offer this limitation as a reason for despair, and I do not think it undermines the value of everything this book has attempted. It is, instead, I think, the most honest note on which a book like this can end. History, practiced carefully, gives us the machinery, the pattern, the institutional failure, and the traceable path by which ordinary suspicion became extraordinary catastrophe. It does not, and cannot, give us back the people themselves, in the full particularity of who they actually were. That particularity is simply lost, for all but a small handful of cases this book has been fortunate enough to examine in any real human detail. What remains for the historian, and for the reader who has followed this book to its end, is the responsibility of holding that loss honestly — neither filling it with invented detail that would flatter our own capacity for empathy, nor treating its absence as a reason to stop caring about what the surviving evidence does, in fact, allow us to know.

There is a particular kind of humility this requires, and I want to name it plainly rather than let it remain implicit. It would be comforting to believe that empathy, sincerely felt, can close the distance between a modern reader and a seventeenth-century prisoner awaiting interrogation. I do not think it can, not fully, and I think a book that claimed otherwise would be offering its readers a false intimacy with the past rather than an honest relationship with it. What empathy can do, and what I have tried to let it do throughout this book, is shape the questions we ask of the evidence and the care with which we handle what it tells us. It cannot substitute for evidence we do not have. Recognizing that limit is not a failure of feeling. It is, I have come to think, feeling's most disciplined and most honest form, applied to a past that cannot answer back and does not owe us the comfort of being fully knowable.

section.subtitle: On the Reader's Part in This
section.paragraph: I have written most of this reflection in the first person, which is not how the rest of this book has spoken, and I want to explain that choice before closing, because I think it matters for what I am asking of you as this book ends. The preceding ten chapters were written to stand on their own, supported by evidence, structured to let the pattern of accusation, prosecution, and confession speak through documented fact rather than through my own voice as its narrator. This final reflection is different by design. It is the place where I step out from behind that evidentiary structure and ask you directly what a book like this is actually for.

I do not think it is only, or even primarily, for the accumulation of historical knowledge, valuable as that accumulation is in its own right. I think a book like this is also, quietly, an invitation to notice the same mechanisms at a smaller and more personal scale, in whatever institutions you yourself move through — the meeting where a conclusion is reached before the evidence is fully heard, the rumor that travels faster and further than any attempt to correct it, the moment when disagreeing with a room's settled consensus requires more than intellectual conviction and asks something closer to what Spee and Weyer and Salazar were eventually asked to give. I am not suggesting an equivalence between any ordinary modern disagreement and the machinery this book has documented; the distance between those things is real, and I have tried throughout this reflection not to collapse it carelessly. I am suggesting only that the discipline this book has modeled — slow down, examine the evidence on its own terms, distrust the conclusion that arrived before the inquiry did — is not a discipline unique to historians working three or four centuries after the fact. It is available now, to you, in whatever room you next find yourself in in which suspicion is gathering faster than evidence can keep pace with it.

section.subtitle: Closing the Book
section.paragraph: I return, one last time, to the farmhouse this book opened with. The fevered child. The frost. The cow that stopped giving milk. I do not know, and this book has never claimed to know, what became of that specific household, because it was never a specific household to begin with — only a composite, built from the patterns this book has spent ten chapters carefully documenting. But I know, because the archive this book has drawn upon tells me so, again and again, in town after town and decade after decade, that households very much like it existed by the thousands, and that in a meaningful number of documented cases, the fear that gathered in rooms very much like that one eventually found its way, through the specific institutional path this book has traced in such deliberate detail, to a courtroom, an interrogation, and in far too many instances, a death.

That is the history this book has tried to tell honestly: not a parable, not a gallery of horrors, not a tidy morality tale with clearly marked villains and heroes, but a specific, documented, and ultimately human catastrophe, built by ordinary institutions under recognizable human pressures, and eventually, slowly, imperfectly dismantled by other ordinary people who found, within those same institutions, the evidence and the courage to say that it had to stop. I do not know what you will carry forward from these pages beyond the facts themselves. But if this book has done its work, I hope it is something like this: a clearer sense of how such machinery is actually built, piece by traceable piece, and a corresponding clearer sense of what, specifically, has to be in place — oversight, doubt, the willingness to look carefully at evidence that makes us uncomfortable — to keep it from being built again.
